passages.title: Family, Media and Peers: What Shapes a Child?
passages.subtitle: How domestic upbringing interacts with television, digital networks, and friendship groups
paragraphs: Developmental psychologists have long debated which forces leave the deepest mark on a child's personality and values. For most of human history, family upbringing stood at the centre of that process. During early childhood, parents and older relatives act as a child's first role model, demonstrating everyday manners, emotional control, and attitudes toward honesty. Even before children enter primary school, they absorb subtle family habits regarding conflict, curiosity, and kindness.

Once formal schooling begins, however, external forces rapidly gain influence. Classmates and friendship circles—collectively known as peers—become powerful mirrors through which young people judge themselves. By early adolescence, the desire for social belonging intensifies, making teenagers especially responsive to peer pressure. While adults often associate peer pressure solely with risky choices such as skipping class or vaping, research shows that peers can exert an equally strong positive pull, motivating teenagers to join study clubs, volunteer, or persist in athletics.

Alongside friendship groups, daily exposure to media—spanning broadcast television, streaming platforms, and social apps—has reshaped modern childhood. Well-produced educational TV documentaries and language programmes can expand vocabulary and nurture tolerance toward unfamiliar cultures. Conversely, prolonged consumption of aggressive entertainment or heavily filtered influencer feeds is linked with shortened attention spans, heightened anxiety, and distorted body image.

Because completely insulating children from television and smartphones is neither realistic nor helpful, media-literacy researchers advocate a structured three-stage strategy called 'active mediation'. First, families agree on consistent household rules—such as keeping screens out of dining rooms and bedrooms. Second, parents practise joint viewing, sitting alongside children during key TV programmes or games to understand what captures their interest. Finally, adults initiate critical conversations, encouraging young viewers to question commercial motives behind advertisements and recognise edited online content.

Crucially, long-term studies suggest that family, peers, and media do not operate in isolation. Children raised in warm, communicative homes tend to choose more supportive friendship groups and feel comfortable discussing troubling online encounters with adults. Far from making parents irrelevant, the modern media landscape makes steady parental guidance more valuable than ever.

passages.title: Elite Sport Funding vs. Grassroots Participation
passages.subtitle: Allocating public sports budgets between Olympic podiums and neighbourhood fitness
paragraphs: When a nation celebrates an unexpected Olympic gold medal, politicians are quick to praise the investment that made victory possible. Yet behind the televised celebrations lies a difficult dilemma in public spending. With national budgets under constant strain, should governments channel hundreds of millions into elite sport programmes designed for a tiny fraction of citizens, or should they prioritise everyday grassroots participation for the broader public?

Advocates of elite funding maintain that international sporting excellence generates extraordinary national pride, fostering social cohesion across diverse communities. Moreover, structured talent development systems—employing biomechanics specialists, nutritionists, and full-time coaches—produce visible sporting heroes. Supporters cite the 'trickle-down effect', claiming that watching domestic champions triumph inspires millions of schoolchildren to take up regular exercise.

Public health researchers, however, have struggled to verify this trickle-down theory. Independent evaluations conducted after several recent Olympic Games found that while club registrations briefly spiked during the tournament month, overall population fitness levels remained unchanged two years later. Meanwhile, rising rates of childhood and adult obesity continue to drive up chronic disease costs for public hospitals. From a health-economics perspective, spending millions per medal appears inefficient when basic neighbourhood sports facilities are closing due to local council cuts.

Grassroots advocates therefore urge governments to redirect funds toward accessible municipal infrastructure: well-lit cycling lanes, free outdoor fitness parks, and subsidised community swimming pools. Unlike elite academies, these spaces welcome beginners, older adults, and low-income families who rarely identify with professional athletes. Even modest increases in daily walking or recreational sport yield substantial reductions in cardiovascular illness and healthcare expenditure.

A parallel debate concerns how seriously children should treat competitive sport. Driven by scholarship hopes and professional academy scouts, some youngsters specialise in a single sport before age twelve, training intensely year-round. While structured competition teaches resilience and teamwork, paediatric sports doctors warn that early over-specialisation raises the risk of overuse injuries and psychological exhaustion, causing many promising teenagers to abandon sport entirely.

Ultimately, framing elite and community sport as mutually exclusive rivals is short-sighted. High-performance champions cannot emerge from nowhere; they begin in school playgrounds and local youth leagues. A balanced sports policy should tie every major investment in elite academies to guaranteed funding for neighbourhood facilities—ensuring that international medals complement, rather than replace, a healthier population.

passages.label: READING PASSAGE 3
passages.instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.
passages.title: Education and Success in Modern Society
passages.subtitle: Redefining achievement beyond university degrees in an era of rapid change
paragraphs: For much of the post-war era, the relationship between education and success appeared straightforward: securing strong university qualifications led reliably to stable corporate employment, rising income, and respected social status. Families invested heavily in higher education under the assumption that a prestigious diploma served as a lifelong passport to prosperity. Today, however, economists and sociologists argue that this neat equation no longer captures how success is built.

Part of the disruption stems from the sheer expansion of higher education—a trend scholars call 'credential inflation'. When barely fifteen percent of young adults graduated from university, a bachelor's degree functioned as an immediate signal of rare capability. In economies where over half of school leavers now earn degrees, employers increasingly treat a university certificate as a basic minimum rather than a guarantee of distinction, leaving many graduates in positions once held by high-school leavers.

Simultaneously, digital technology has lowered the barriers to entrepreneurship. Creative individuals with modest capital can now build software tools, launch e-commerce brands, or monetise specialist media channels directly from a laptop. High-profile founders who succeeded without completing traditional degrees have challenged the cultural assumption that formal academic credentials are the sole measure of intelligence or ambition.

When researchers examine what truly distinguishes high achievers across diverse fields—from artisan craftspeople to medical scientists—one psychological trait appears repeatedly: determination. Psychologist Angela Duckworth's work on 'grit' demonstrates that sustained persistence in the face of setbacks often predicts long-term accomplishment more accurately than raw test scores alone. Talent opens doors, but resilience and deliberate practice determine who progresses when initial plans collapse.

Equally decisive in the modern economy is lifelong learning. Because artificial intelligence, green energy, and digital platforms continuously transform workplace tasks, knowledge acquired at age twenty-two depreciates rapidly. Thriving professionals treat formal graduation not as the finish line of education, but as its starting point—regularly acquiring micro-credentials, switching disciplines, and seeking peer mentorship throughout their working lives.

None of this renders university obsolete. Regulated fields such as surgery, civil engineering, and scientific research still rightly demand rigorous degrees, and higher education offers unmatched opportunities for intellectual growth. Yet society is gradually embracing a broader, healthier definition of success—one measured not merely by paper qualifications, but by adaptability, purposeful work, and the determination to keep learning.
